topics.title: Ecology and the idea of a population

learn.hook: No tiger lives alone in an ecological sense. It belongs to a population whose births, deaths and movements decide its future.
points: Ecology is the study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical (abiotic) environment.
Ecology deals with four levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities and biomes.

A population is a group of individuals of a species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources, and potentially interbreeding. Examples: all lotus plants in a pond, rats in an abandoned building or teakwood trees in a forest tract. For asexually reproducing organisms, interbreeding is not considered.
Population ecology is important because it links ecology to population genetics and evolution. Natural selection operates at the population level to evolve the desired traits.

example.q: Which of these is a population: (a) all birds in a forest, (b) all Indian peafowl in Gir National Park, (c) all plants in a garden?
steps: A population must be one species in a defined area.
(a) and (c) include many species.
(b) is one species (Pavo cristatus) in a defined area.
example.answer: (b) All Indian peafowl in Gir National Park

learn.reallife: Project Tiger, launched in 1973, treats tigers in each reserve as populations to be monitored and managed.

topics.title: Birth rate, death rate and sex ratio

learn.hook: If 8 new lotus plants appear in a pond that had 20, the birth rate is 0.4 per lotus per year. Population maths is that direct.
points: A population has attributes that an individual does not: an individual is born and dies, but a population has birth rates and death rates. These are expressed per capita (per individual of the population).
Birth rate example: a pond had 20 lotus plants last year, and 8 new plants were added, making 28. Birth rate = 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.
Death rate example: in a lab population of 40 fruit flies, 4 died in a week. Death rate = 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week.
Sex ratio is another attribute: an individual is male or female, but a population has a sex ratio, e.g. 60 per cent females and 40 per cent males.

example.q: A population of 500 deer had 150 births and 50 deaths in a year. Find the per capita birth rate and death rate.
steps: Birth rate = births/population = 150/500 = 0.3 per deer per year.
Death rate = deaths/population = 50/500 = 0.1 per deer per year.
example.answer: Birth rate 0.3; death rate 0.1 (per deer per year)

learn.reallife: India's Census reports birth rates, death rates and sex ratio, attributes of the population, not of any single person.

topics.title: Age pyramids and measuring population size

learn.hook: Census pyramids show why India's working-age population is huge: the shape of the pyramid tells the story of a nation's future.
points: A population at any given time has individuals of different ages. Plotting the age distribution (per cent individuals of a given age or age group) gives an age pyramid. Age groups: pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive. For humans, age pyramids usually show males and females in a combined diagram.
The shape reflects growth status: expanding (triangular, with a broad pre-reproductive base), stable (bell-shaped) and declining (urn-shaped, with fewer pre-reproductive individuals).

Population size (population density, N) is measured in different ways. Total number is often best, but not always meaningful: 200 Parthenium plants versus one huge banyan tree with a large canopy. Here per cent cover or biomass is more meaningful.

If counting is impossible or time-consuming, relative densities can serve, e.g. number of fish caught per trap in a lake. Population sizes are often estimated indirectly: tiger census in national parks and tiger reserves is based on pug marks and faecal pellets.

example.q: An age pyramid has a very broad base of children and a narrow top of elderly people. What is its shape and what does it show?
steps: A broad pre-reproductive base with narrowing upper bars gives a triangle.
Many young individuals will enter the reproductive group.
example.answer: Triangular (expanding) pyramid; the population is growing.

learn.reallife: The All India Tiger Estimation uses camera traps along with pug marks and scat surveys, an advanced form of indirect census.

topics.title: Population growth and the exponential model

learn.hook: With unlimited food, a few bacteria can outgrow a stadium in days. That is exponential growth.
points: Population density changes due to four basic processes: natality (B), the number of births added; mortality (D), deaths; immigration (I), individuals of the same species coming in; and emigration (E), individuals leaving. Natality and immigration increase density; mortality and emigration decrease it.
If N is density at time t, density at time t + 1 is Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. Density increases if B + I is more than D + E.

Exponential growth occurs when resources (food and space) are unlimited. If b and d are per capita birth and death rates, dN/dt = (b − d) × N; with r = b − d, dN/dt = rN. In integral form, Nₜ = N₀ eʳᵗ, where e is the base of natural logarithms (2.71828). Plotting N against time gives a J-shaped curve.

r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, an important parameter for assessing biotic or abiotic impacts on population growth. Examples: Norway rat r = 0.015, flour beetle r = 0.12. In 1981, r for India's human population was 0.0205.
Practice type: apply Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)] and dN/dt = rN; draw and interpret age pyramids; calculate per capita birth and death rates.

example.q: A population of 1000 has 120 births, 30 immigrants, 70 deaths and 20 emigrants in a year. Find the population the next year.
steps: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]

learn.reallife: Planners at NITI Aayog use growth-rate models to project India's future population for schools, jobs and healthcare.

quiz.explain: Births and arrivals add individuals; deaths and departures remove them.

teach.praise: Super! Births and immigration add, deaths and emigration subtract; with unlimited resources dN/dt = rN gives a J-shaped curve.
teach.nudge: Good! Write the equation for exponential growth and say what r means.

learn.hook: No population can grow forever. Every habitat has a limit, called the carrying capacity, just as a train compartment has a limit on how many passengers it can safely hold.
points: No population has unlimited resources, so exponential growth cannot continue. Resources are limited, causing competition among individuals and survival of the fittest.
In a given habitat, resources can support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible: the carrying capacity (K).

A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows an initial lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when population density reaches the carrying capacity. Plotting N against time gives a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve. This is Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth: dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K].
Since resources for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic growth model is considered more realistic.

Graph comparison: the J-shaped curve (exponential, unlimited resources) keeps rising steeply; the S-shaped curve (logistic) levels off at K. When N is much smaller than K, (K − N)/K is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential.

example.q: For a population with r = 0.2, K = 1000 and N = 500, calculate dN/dt using the logistic equation.
steps: dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K]

learn.reallife: Fisheries departments set catch limits based on carrying capacity so that fish stocks in reservoirs like Hirakud are not overexploited.

learn.hook: A bamboo plant may grow for decades, flower once in a spectacular burst and then die, a life-history strategy very different from a mango tree's.
points: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness (high r value), in the habitat where they live.
Under a particular set of selection pressures, organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy.
Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime, like Pacific salmon fish and bamboo; others breed many times during their lifetime, like most birds and mammals.
Some produce a large number of small-sized offspring, like oysters and pelagic fishes; others produce a small number of large-sized offspring, like birds and mammals.
Ecologists suggest life history traits of organisms have evolved in relation to the constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat in which they live.

example.q: Classify: (a) bamboo, (b) a pelagic fish, (c) a dog, by breeding frequency or offspring number and size.
steps: (a) Bamboo breeds only once in a lifetime.
(b) Pelagic fish produce many small offspring.
(c) Dogs (mammals) breed many times and produce few large offspring.
example.answer: (a) breeds once (b) many small offspring (c) breeds many times, few large offspring

learn.reallife: Mass flowering of Melocanna bamboo in Mizoram, about every 48 years, leads to rat population explosions called 'mautam', showing how life history affects whole ecosystems.

learn.hook: When prickly pear cactus overran millions of hectares in Australia, the fix was not a chemical but a cactus-eating moth from its native home.
points: Interspecific interactions: mutualism (+, +), competition (−, −), predation (+, −), parasitism (+, −), commensalism (+, 0) and amensalism (−, 0). Both species benefit in mutualism and both lose in competition.

Predation is nature's way of transferring energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels. Predators keep prey populations under control; without them prey could reach very high densities. The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s spread over millions of hectares and was controlled only after a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat was introduced.

Predators help maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey species. When the starfish Pisaster was removed from an enclosed intertidal area in an American experiment, more than 10 invertebrate species became extinct within a year due to interspecific competition. Predators in nature are 'prudent', since overexploiting prey could drive both prey and predator to extinction.

Prey defences: some insects and frogs are cryptically coloured (camouflaged); the monarch butterfly is distasteful to birds due to a chemical acquired by feeding on a poisonous weed as a caterpillar. For plants, herbivores are predators; nearly 25 per cent of insects are phytophagous. Thorns of Acacia and cactus are morphological defences. Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats do not browse on it. Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are chemicals plants produce as defences against grazers and browsers.

example.q: Why are cattle and goats rarely seen browsing on Calotropis growing in abandoned fields?
steps: Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides.
These chemicals defend the plant against herbivores.
example.answer: Its poisonous cardiac glycosides deter grazing animals.

learn.reallife: Wildlife managers in India note that tigers and leopards keep deer and wild boar numbers in check; where predators vanish, crop raiding by herbivores rises.

quiz.explain: One species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited.

learn.hook: Five kinds of warblers can share one tree without fighting, simply by feeding in different parts of it.
points: Competition is often thought to occur between closely related species for limited resources, but unrelated species can compete too: flamingos and resident fishes in some shallow South American lakes compete for zooplankton. Resources need not be limiting: in interference competition, one species' feeding efficiency drops due to the inhibitory presence of another even when resources are abundant.

Competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured by its r) is significantly lower in the presence of another species. The Abingdon tortoise of the Galapagos became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, apparently due to the goats' greater browsing efficiency.

Competitive release: a species restricted to a small area by a competitively superior species expands its range dramatically when the competitor is removed. Connell's field experiments on rocky sea coasts of Scotland showed that the larger, superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chthamalus (spelt Chathamalus in NCERT).

Gause's competitive exclusion principle: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually. This may hold if resources are limiting, but not otherwise.

Resource partitioning: competing species can coexist by choosing different times for feeding or different foraging patterns. MacArthur showed five closely related warbler species living on the same tree avoided competition through behavioural differences in foraging.

example.q: Barnacle species X occupies only the upper rocks; when species Y is removed from the lower rocks, X spreads downward. What is this phenomenon, and which experiment showed it?
steps: X was restricted by competitively superior Y.
Removing Y lets X expand its range.
example.answer: Competitive release; Connell's barnacle experiments (Balanus and Chthamalus) in Scotland.

learn.reallife: In India's grasslands, invasive species sometimes outcompete native grasses; ecologists use competition theory to plan restoration.

learn.hook: A koel lays its eggs in a crow's nest and lets the crow raise its chicks, and its eggs are even coloured to fool the host.
points: Parasitism evolved because it provides free lodging and meals. Many parasites are host-specific (can parasitise only a single species of host), so host and parasite tend to co-evolve: if the host evolves a mechanism to reject the parasite, the parasite must evolve to counter it.
Adaptations of parasites: loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs or suckers to cling to the host, loss of the digestive system and high reproductive capacity.

Life cycles are often complex. The human liver fluke (a trematode) depends on two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish, to complete its life cycle. The malarial parasite needs a vector (mosquito) to spread. Parasites harm the host: they may reduce survival, growth and reproduction, lower population density and make the host weaker and more vulnerable to predation.

Ectoparasites feed on the external surface of the host: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on many marine fish. Cuscuta, a parasitic plant on hedge plants, has lost its chlorophyll and leaves and derives nutrition from the host. Endoparasites live inside the host's body (liver, kidney, lungs, red blood cells) and have simplified morphology and anatomy with high reproductive potential.

Brood parasitism in birds: the parasitic bird lays eggs in the host's nest and lets the host incubate them, e.g. the cuckoo (koel) in a crow's nest. The parasite's eggs have evolved to resemble the host's in size and colour, reducing the chance of rejection.

example.q: Explain how the cuckoo's eggs show co-evolution with the crow.
steps: The cuckoo lays eggs in the crow's nest (brood parasitism).
Crows that detect foreign eggs would eject them.
Cuckoo eggs evolved to resemble crow eggs in size and colour, reducing detection.
example.answer: Egg mimicry evolved in response to the host's ability to reject foreign eggs.

learn.reallife: The 'kuhoo' call of the Asian koel in Indian summers is familiar; few people realise it is a brood parasite raised by crows.

quiz.explain: The trematode depends on two intermediate hosts: a snail and a fish.

quiz.q: Cuscuta is an example of
options: an ectoparasite that has lost chlorophyll and leaves
quiz.explain: Cuscuta grows on hedge plants and draws nutrition from them.

quiz.q: The cuckoo laying its eggs in a crow's nest is an example of
quiz.explain: The host incubates and raises the parasite's young.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a typical adaptation of parasites?
quiz.explain: Parasites tend to lose unnecessary sense organs.

quiz.q: Why do host and parasite tend to co-evolve?
options: Many parasites are host-specific, so if the host evolves resistance, the parasite must evolve a counter-mechanism
quiz.explain: Their close association drives reciprocal evolution.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the arms race

quiz.q: Ticks on dogs are
quiz.explain: They feed on the external surface of the host.

quiz.q: The eggs of brood parasites resemble the host's eggs in size and colour to
options: reduce the chance of the host detecting and ejecting them
quiz.explain: Egg mimicry is an adaptation to avoid rejection.

quiz.q: Endoparasites generally have
options: complex digestive systems and few offspring
simplified morphology and anatomy with high reproductive potential
quiz.explain: Living inside the host favours simplification and high fecundity.
quiz.mistake: Assumes complexity increases inside a host

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is parasitism, how are parasites adapted, and what is a brood parasite?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Parasites co-evolve with hosts, have suckers and high reproduction, can be ecto- or endoparasites, and cuckoos are brood parasites.
teach.nudge: Good! Name one ectoparasite and one adaptation of parasites.

learn.hook: Every fig species has its own wasp partner. Lose the wasp and the fig cannot set seed; lose the fig and the wasp has nowhere to breed.
points: Commensalism (+, 0): one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited. Examples: an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch; barnacles on the back of a whale; the cattle egret foraging near grazing cattle, which flush out insects; clown fish living among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone for protection, with no apparent benefit to the anemone.

Mutualism (+, +): lichens are an intimate mutualism between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria. Mycorrhizae are associations of fungi with roots of higher plants: fungi help absorb nutrients and plants provide carbohydrates.

Plant–animal mutualisms: plants offer pollen, nectar and fruits as rewards to pollinators and seed dispersers. Many fig species have tight one-to-one relationships with pollinator wasps: the female wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for egg-laying sites, and uses developing seeds to nourish her larvae.

Sexual deceit: the Mediterranean orchid Ophrys has a petal resembling the female bee in size, colour and markings. The male bee pseudocopulates with the flower and gets dusted with pollen, transferring it to another flower. If the female bee's appearance changes even slightly during evolution, the orchid must co-evolve to maintain pollination success.

Exercise type: identify interactions from examples (e.g. cattle egret = commensalism, lichen = mutualism, Cuscuta = parasitism, Balanus vs Chthamalus = competition); list plant defences against herbivores; explain competitive exclusion.

example.q: Identify the interaction: (a) orchid on a mango branch, (b) lichen, (c) cattle egret and cattle, (d) fig and wasp.
steps: (a) Orchid benefits, mango unaffected: commensalism.
(b) Fungus and alga both benefit: mutualism.
(c) Egret benefits, cattle unaffected: commensalism.
(d) Both benefit: mutualism.

learn.reallife: Bagulas (cattle egrets) following tractors and buffaloes in Indian fields are a classic everyday example of commensalism.

quiz.q: The relationship between a cattle egret and grazing cattle is an example of
quiz.explain: Egrets catch insects flushed out by cattle; cattle are unaffected.

quiz.q: Lichens represent
options: mutualism between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria
quiz.explain: Both partners benefit in lichens.

quiz.q: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys gets pollinated by
options: sexual deceit, with a petal resembling a female bee
quiz.explain: Male bees pseudocopulate with the flower and transfer pollen.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Ophrys offers a nectar reward

quiz.q: In the fig–wasp relationship, the female wasp
options: pollinates the fig and uses its developing seeds to nourish her larvae
harms the fig without any benefit to it
quiz.explain: Both species benefit: a tight mutualism.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the wasp is a parasite only

quiz.q: The clown fish living among sea anemone tentacles is an example of
options: mutualism with clear benefit to the anemone
quiz.explain: The fish gets protection; the anemone appears not to benefit.

quiz.q: An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch shows
quiz.explain: The orchid benefits from support; the mango is not harmed.

quiz.q: In mycorrhiza, the plant provides the fungus with
quiz.explain: The fungus helps nutrient absorption and receives carbohydrates.

quiz.q: If the female bee's colour pattern changes during evolution, the Ophrys orchid must
options: co-evolve to maintain its resemblance and pollination success
quiz.explain: Pollination by deceit depends on close mimicry.
